prResults.title: Include adp usage policy reference
prResults.whatItAdds: Not a new skill/capability — an incremental documentation update to the existing orbis-adp-consume skill (plugin version bumped 1.0.6 -> 1.0.7). It adds an "ADP USAGE POLICY" section to SKILL.md that teaches Claude the Analytical Data Plane (ADP) fair-use rules: max 2 parallel queries per user, 10-minute query timeout, no automated/keep-alive usage, no personal compute on the central ADP workspace, and whitelisted exemptions (MAA PowerBI dashboards, MyTomTom). It tells Claude to surface the policy proactively on the first query and on heavy/automated/large-scale queries, explains that breaching quotas auto-cancels queries (reason posted to #analytical-data-plane-notifications) and that repeated violations lead to access revocation, and steers big/heavy/automated workloads to BYOC (the user's own Databricks workspace), which is exempt from the central quotas. Also adds a pre-query assessment checklist, a troubleshooting-table row for unexpectedly cancelled queries, and a clarifying note that these quotas apply only to the central ADP SQL warehouse, not BYOC. Links to the full policy on Confluence (MANA space).
prResults.readyToUse: Ready to use. It is a small, self-contained documentation refinement (~46 added lines, no deletions, no code/script changes) to a skill already published in catalog/ — clearly a mature, in-use skill. The change mirrors the same edits into both the source skills/ path and the catalog/ copy and bumps the version, so it is mergeable as-is. Reviewer caveat: editing catalog/ directly contradicts the PR template's "no changes to catalog/ — the bot writes those" guideline, which may need a maintainer to resolve, but the content itself is final, not experimental.
prResults.relevanceToRefinement: Low. The work loop (Pick -> Research -> Plan -> Build -> Verify -> Share) is about refining and building an arbitrary backlog feature with Claude. The parent orbis-adp skill is only useful to a team whose chosen feature happens to require querying TomTom analytics/metrics data via Databricks SQL — a narrow data-access use case, not a general feature-building aid. This PR is narrower still: it only adds usage-policy guardrails to that already-existing skill, adding no new capability for refining or building features. It would matter only to a team building something that consumes ADP data, and even then mostly as cost/compliance hygiene rather than as a refinement tool.

prResults.title: feat: removed dev references from lanemodel in mcr skill
prResults.whatItAdds: The PR updates an existing plugin/skill (orbis-mcr, version 1.0.4 -> 1.0.5), it does not add a new one. The underlying skill connects Claude Code and the GitHub Copilot CLI to TomTom's Map Central Repository (MCR) so a coding agent can run SQL queries against TomTom Orbis map data via Databricks SQL (a packaged query_mcr.py helper handles auth, region/catalog selection, BYOC via your own Unity Catalog workspace, polling, and cost guardrails). This specific PR refines how the Lane Model product is exposed: it renames the product olm -> lanemodel, removes the old "early-access only / requires special permissions / auto-route to Dev environment" coupling, recasts Dev as just a normal selectable region (--region dev, labelled non-production) instead of an early-access channel, replaces the old per-product table with an authoritative product x region availability matrix (nexventura, nexkorea, adhoc, bifrost, lanemodel), and adds a pre-query validation step that checks the product/region combination before building a query (e.g. refuse lanemodel for Korea). Also minor: query_mcr.py --region choices now derived from list(REGIONS) and help-text cleanup; README/plugin.json wording and version bump. Based directly on the diff.
prResults.readyToUse: Ready to use and mature. The base skill is at v1.x with a working query_mcr.py script and is already published in the catalog. This PR is itself a de-experimentalizing change: it promotes lanemodel from "early access only, requires special permissions, auto-routed to Dev" to a normal selectable production product, which is a signal of increasing maturity rather than experimental status. PR is OPEN, not draft. The change is documentation/behavior-correctness only, low risk.
prResults.relevanceToRefinement: Specialized data-access capability rather than a general feature-refinement aid. It is directly useful in the Research/Build phases only when the backlog feature actually touches TomTom Orbis map data (querying Road Model / Lane Model / Korea map tables from the agent). At a maps company that is a real but minority subset of feature teams, so it is niche-but-mature. The PR contents themselves are a small refinement; the score reflects the skill's usefulness, not the diff size.

prResults.title: Add jira-tree skill (assigned-tickets hierarchy tree)
prResults.whatItAdds: A single-skill plugin (`jira-tree`, category project-management) that renders the current user's recent/assigned Jira tickets as a hierarchy tree — epics → stories → sub-tasks — with linked/dependent items (blocks, blocked-by, clones, bug-of, relates) marked inline via status and link icons, followed by a "loose ends" pass (Done tickets blocking still-open work; the user's open tickets blocking downstream work). Triggered by `/jira-tree`. It queries the Atlassian MCP with `searchJiraIssuesUsingJql` (`assignee = currentUser() ORDER BY updated DESC`), excludes the `description` field (token-limit overflow), paginates up to a 5-page (~500 issue) safety cap (announcing truncation rather than silently dropping), and parses each saved page with a bundled jq snippet. An optional argument is folded in as an extra JQL filter (e.g. `/jira-tree project = NAV`, `status != Done`, `updated >= -30d`). It is purely read/overview — it complements the existing authoring skill `jira-ticket-writer`.
prResults.readyToUse: Ready-to-use in substance, but the PR is still a DRAFT (state OPEN, isDraft true). The skill is complete and self-contained: full YAML frontmatter with rich trigger phrases, detailed step-by-step instructions, the TomTom cloud ID (1cca41ed-…) hard-coded so it works for any TomTom user out of the box, pagination/truncation handling, and a working jq parser. The generated catalog files (plugin.json, README, marketplace.json entry, CODEOWNERS) are all present and consistent. There are no scripts/binaries to break — it relies only on the model + jq + the Atlassian MCP. The sole runtime dependency is an active Atlassian MCP connection. Author flagged one open question (individual vs team `author`/owner). So: functionally mergeable/usable, pending un-drafting and reviewer sign-off.
prResults.relevanceToRefinement: Moderately relevant. It directly supports the "Pick" stage of the loop — surfacing a participant's assigned backlog tickets, showing the epic/story/sub-task hierarchy of a candidate feature, and exposing blockers/dependencies before committing to refine one. The loose-ends pass adds useful situational awareness about what a ticket blocks or is blocked by. However, it is read-only Jira reporting: it does not help Research, Plan, Build, or Verify the feature itself (no code, no spec generation, no ticket authoring — that is jira-tree's sibling jira-ticket-writer). So it is a helpful orientation/selection aid at the start of the track rather than a core driver of the refine-and-build work.

prResults.title: Add reliable-deck-builder plugin
prResults.whatItAdds: A pure-skill plugin (category: general) that encodes a gated, five-phase workflow for building slide decks/presentations that "survive scrutiny" — board, financial, and leadership decks where every number must be defensible. Phases: (1) Plan — elicit and play back the audience, one-sentence narrative, presenter's perspective, and the ask BEFORE touching data; (2) Sources — anchor to trusted inputs, never invent numbers, never blend plan with actuals unlabeled; (3) Structure — narrative skeleton/outline approved before any slide is built; (4) Creation — build in passes (outline → per-slide content with source refs → render via python-pptx), mark assumptions visibly; (5) Verification — an INDEPENDENT, cross-model hostile reviewer tries to break the numbers/logic/narrative, then human sign-off. Ships SKILL.md, reviewer-prompt.md (the hostile-reviewer prompt), and challenge.sh — a working bash script that pipes the prompt + deck text + sources into GitHub Copilot CLI (copilot -p, headless, GPT-based) as a different-model-family challenger, with documented fallbacks (fresh Claude subagent or M365 Copilot) and clean exit codes (2 = Copilot CLI unavailable). Includes a risk gradient (Low/Medium/High) that dials rigor, a quick-reference, common-mistakes table, and red-flag STOP triggers.
prResults.readyToUse: Ready-to-use. Not a draft; state OPEN, version 1.0.0. Complete and self-consistent: full SKILL.md (88 lines), a functional challenge.sh with binary resolution, sandboxing flags, and graceful fallbacks, and a reviewer-prompt.md. plugin.json, plugin-definitions yaml, README, marketplace.json entry, catalog/ tree, and CODEOWNERS are all present and validate.py reportedly passes locally. Caveat: the PR body claims "catalog/ and marketplace.json are intentionally untouched — left for CI to generate," but the diff actually includes both the generated catalog/ tree and the marketplace.json edit, so the body is slightly inaccurate (harmless — content is correct). The Verification phase depends on GitHub Copilot CLI + a Copilot subscription to get true cross-model review; without it you fall back to a fresh Claude/M365 context.
prResults.relevanceToRefinement: Domain mismatch but one transferable pattern. The conference track is about refining/building a real backlog SOFTWARE feature (Pick→Research→Plan→Build→Verify→Share); this skill builds presentation decks, which an engineer would not reach for while implementing a feature. It is not packaged to plan, build, or verify code. The genuinely relevant overlap is conceptual: its gated Plan→Build→Verify loop and especially its Verify step — an independent, fresh-context, cross-model hostile review that tries to BREAK the work before declaring it done — is exactly the discipline the track's Verify phase wants, and challenge.sh is a concrete, reusable mechanism for driving a cross-model adversarial reviewer (GitHub Copilot CLI) that engineers could adapt to review a feature/PR rather than a deck. There is also a tangential fit with the track's "Share" step if a team wants to produce a defensible results/demo deck. Net: useful as an inspiration/reference for the verification pattern, and directly grabbable only for the Share-the-results sub-task — not for the core feature-building loop.

prResults.title: feat: add orbis ogp support to the orbis-mcr skill
prResults.whatItAdds: Refines the already-shipped orbis-mcr skill (a plugin that queries TomTom Orbis map data in the Map Central Repository via Databricks SQL) to support a second data model: Orbis OGP, the Overture-aligned product living in the sibling schema map_central_repository_orbis_ogp. The change is almost entirely instructional/documentation in SKILL.md (bumps plugin version 1.0.4 to 1.0.5): adds a DATA MODELS section comparing 3G (default, 4 generic tag-based tables per product) vs OGP (themed tables, typed columns, WKB geometry, bbox, no tags map, no h3_index); a routing rule (default to 3G, only switch to OGP on explicit signals like "OGP"/"Overture"/"orbis_ogp"); version-discovery SQL (OGP table names embed version e.g. transportation_segment_orbis_ogp_26190_000, don't hardcode); a link to the external Orbis OGP spec (llms.txt); and per-schema variants of the common explore operations. The bundled query_mcr.py change is purely top-of-file docstring/usage comments adding an OGP example; no executable logic changed.
prResults.readyToUse: Yes, ready to use. It is a documentation refinement of an already-shipped, versioned skill, and OGP is described as a live global product (not early-access like olm). Caveat: actual usability depends on the user having a Databricks token and OGP schema access in their region; I could not verify the schema is populated without querying (needs tokens). Merge-process friction: the PR hand-edits files under catalog/ and .claude-plugin/, which the PR's own checklist says are bot-written and should not be changed manually; this may cause CI/sync friction but does not affect the capability.
prResults.relevanceToRefinement: Narrow domain fit. It is a map-data access tool that helps mainly in the Research phase, and only for the subset of conference teams whose backlog feature actually needs to query Orbis/Overture map data via Databricks SQL. For the generic "refine and build any backlog feature" audience it is not broadly useful; the OGP addition is an incremental polish to that already-narrow skill rather than a new general-purpose capability. Score 3 only if you assume most attending teams are map-feature teams who would hit MCR during research.

prResults.title: feat:(pr-green) make pr green skill
prResults.whatItAdds: Adds one new skill, plugins/pr-tooling/skills/make-pr-green/SKILL.md (1755 lines), and registers it in CLAUDE.md and README.md. It is a continuous, operator-in-the-loop process that drives an existing PR to fully green. Each loop iteration runs three things in parallel: a CI-status check, a set of code-review agents, and a read of existing PR comments; it then posts findings as GitHub PR comments, each carrying a machine-readable action: directive. The GitHub comment thread (not any local file) is the source of truth for what to do; the local markdown is a read-only summary. It classifies each finding (TRIVIAL MINOR / TRIVIAL MAJOR / DIFFICULT MAJOR), then applies fixes, posts replies, commits/pushes, and resolves threads according to action codes F/f/R/r/i/n/X/D/d, looping until all threads are resolved and CI is green or the operator says stop. Notable depth: dynamic per-change agent selection (skips irrelevant lenses, adds up to 3 ad-hoc lenses, always forces correctness on code changes, always adds a simplify lens), a review-base optimization that auto-skips re-review when nothing significant changed, an anti-slop self-critique gate on any prose it authors, a Phase E that verifies the PR title/description against commit history + diff + code, and a D/d contact protocol that uses git blame/log to suggest reviewers and optionally pings them on Slack. Flags: --no-review, --fast-review, --review-standard, --cautious, --auto, --force-auto, --open-browser, --dry-run. Dependencies (enforced at Setup): gh CLI authenticated and the multi-agent-code-review plugin installed (it extracts that plugin's agent roster and prompt template). The review specialists are Java-leaning: buildRosterThunk hardcodes the language to Java and loads a javaSpecPath; the CI/comment loop itself is language-agnostic.
prResults.readyToUse: Complete-but-unmerged. The SKILL.md is functionally complete and detailed, and it already appears as an available skill in this environment. But the PR itself is an open DRAFT (isDraft: true) with an unfilled template body (no What/Why, Implements: NAV- left blank), so it is not formally merge-ready yet. Grab-and-use at a short event is gated by two real prerequisites in the diff: the multi-agent-code-review plugin must be installed (Setup stops if missing) plus gh must be authenticated, and the review specialists assume Java.
prResults.relevanceToRefinement: Lands at the tail of the Pick -> Research -> Plan -> Build -> Verify -> Share loop. It is directly useful for Verify and Share: once a team has built a real backlog feature and opened a PR, this drives that PR to green (fixes CI, addresses review comments, keeps the PR description accurate) without quitting until it is mergeable. It does not help with the core refine/research/plan work itself, so it is adjacent to the track's center rather than at it, but a real feature implies a real PR that must go green, which makes it a strong supporting tool for finishing the conference exercise. Scored 4, not 5, because polish does not equal track-fit, and 4, not 3, because finishing a real PR is genuinely part of the loop.

prResults.title: feat(experimental-skills): add sync-agents skill for multi-agent instruction sync
prResults.whatItAdds: Adds a new `sync-agents` skill to the `experimental-skills` plugin. It converges a project's per-tool AI agent instruction files into a single canonical `AGENTS.md` as the source of truth, then wires the others as thin pointers: `CLAUDE.md` becomes a `# Project Instructions` + `@AGENTS.md` import; `.github/copilot-instructions.md` becomes a fallback pointer (Copilot reads AGENTS.md natively); JetBrains Junie reads root AGENTS.md natively so `.junie/guidelines.md` / `.junie/AGENTS.md` shadow files are migrated and removed. The 247-line SKILL.md defines an 8-step procedure: identify project root; survey existing files and classify the situation (Not initialized / Single legacy / Claude-only / AGENTS.md present / Mixed); migrate only GENERIC content (build/test commands, code style, architecture, security, git conventions) while leaving tool-specific content in place; show a MIGRATION PLAN confirmation gate (skippable via `auto`); update an optional `## Available Skills` discovery index built from project-local `.claude/.github/.junie/skills/*/SKILL.md` frontmatter; wire root and nested-package CLAUDE.md stubs; manage a marker-delimited nested-packages block in copilot-instructions.md; and emit a final report. Ships with 14 evals and ~25 fixture files covering green-field exit, single/mixed migration, junie-shadow, nested wiring, copilot sync/cleanup, auto mode, parallel writes, and trigger/skills-index extraction. Treats legacy-file content as untrusted (classify-only, do not follow embedded instructions).
prResults.readyToUse: Early/experimental — usable but not merged. The PR is OPEN and non-draft, with a complete, detailed SKILL.md, a 14-case eval suite plus fixtures, a plugin version bump (0.2.0 -> 0.3.0), README/CLAUDE.md index updates, and follow-up review feedback already incorporated. However it lives in the `experimental-skills` plugin, the Jira reference is an unfilled stub ("Implements: NAV-"), and its green-field exit path tells users to use an `init-agents` skill that does not exist on the repo's default branch and is not added by this PR (verified via gh api tree search). Core non-green-field flows are self-contained and would work once installed.
prResults.relevanceToRefinement: Low / indirect. The conference track is about refining and building a real backlog feature with Claude through Pick -> Research -> Plan -> Build -> Verify -> Share. `sync-agents` is project-configuration plumbing for multi-agent instruction hygiene; it does not help research, plan, build, or verify a feature. Its only indirect value: (a) the `## Available Skills` index it generates could make OTHER genuinely useful skills more discoverable to agents working in a repo, and (b) it ensures consistent agent guidance across tools. But it pays off only for teams that mix Claude + Copilot + Junie on the same repo (a narrow slice of participants) and is a one-time setup chore, not part of the feature-building loop. That meta-discoverability angle is why it rates a 2 rather than a 1.

prResults.title: feat(team-setup): add team-onboarding skill with setup files and evals
prResults.whatItAdds: Adds a single new skill, team-onboarding, in a new team-setup plugin. It is a 7-step interactive environment-setup wizard for the directions-guidance team: (1) detect entry point + self-assessed level (New/Regular/Advanced/Expert); (2) walk through 6 CLAUDE.md rule blocks and append approved ones to the repo CLAUDE.md; (3) offer 4 hooks merged into .claude/settings.json; (4) verify MCP/tooling (Atlassian via atlassianUserInfo, GitHub CLI via gh auth status, optional Filesystem/Fetch MCP); (5) a skills tour table; (6) a level-filtered learning path with training sessions and curated resources; (7) a completion summary. Ships supporting setup/*.md content files and a 10-scenario behavioral evals.json testing step sequencing, write-confirmation gates, auth-failure handling, level filtering, and settings-merge safety. The SKILL.md is well-structured with explicit confirm-before-write gates. Note the bundled CLAUDE.md rules are tuned to this team's localization workflow (.po files, sample .txt regeneration, NavSDK vs HCP3, locale scope) rather than generic feature work, which limits transfer.
prResults.readyToUse: Early/experimental. plugin.json is version 0.1.0, and the new team-onboarding skill itself is internally coherent (clear steps, supporting files present, 10 evals). However the wider package it presents is not consistent with the repo: marketplace.json only registers the new team-setup plugin, yet the bundled skills-tour.md instructs users to run /plugin install pr-tooling@guidance-ai-tools and marks splitting-big-prs as LIVE, and the README/CLAUDE.md table edits add a pr-tooling row — a plugin this PR neither creates nor registers in the marketplace. The skills-tour also lists 6 further skills (translate-fix, pr-fix, investigate-ticket, run-tests, ci-fixer, review) explicitly as PLANNED, i.e. not delivered here. So the team-onboarding skill is runnable, but it points users at an install path and catalogue that this repo does not yet provide.
prResults.relevanceToRefinement: Indirect / pre-loop. The skill does not serve any phase of the Pick -> Research -> Plan -> Build -> Verify -> Share loop on a backlog feature; it is an environment enabler that gets an engineer's CLAUDE.md, hooks, and MCP set up before that loop. Good setup helps downstream, so it is not irrelevant, but it is one step removed from refining/building a feature, and its concrete CLAUDE.md rules are localization-specific rather than generic, further limiting use at a general feature-refinement track.

prResults.title: feat(jira-tooling): add jira-handover and jira-resume skills
prResults.whatItAdds: A new `jira-tooling` plugin with two Claude Code skills plus a shared reference file (shared/common.md). jira-handover wraps up an AI work session into a JIRA ticket: collects context from the conversation (accomplished / in progress / blockers / next steps / key decisions / file:line entry points / git state), pushes unpushed branches, optionally opens draft PRs, writes a dated handover markdown file (YYYYMMDD_AI_handover_<slug>.md), uploads it as a JIRA attachment via curl, links open PRs as remote issue links, and posts a summary comment. jira-resume does the reverse: fetches the ticket, finds the newest *AI_handover*.md attachment, downloads and displays it, offers to restore the recorded git branch, and surfaces Next Steps as a checklist. Every JIRA/git write is gated behind explicit user confirmation; documented fallbacks (embed content in comment, paste manually) handle missing creds or upload failures.
prResults.readyToUse: Ready-to-use but early. State OPEN, not a draft, authored by the conference organizer (Michal Slonina). Structurally complete: plugin.json, full SKILL.md bodies for both skills, shared/common.md, registered in marketplace.json + CLAUDE.md + README, and includes behavioral evals (6 cases for handover, 4 for resume) and trigger evals (8 each). Caveats: version 0.1.0, still unmerged/unreviewed, and the attachment-upload and remote-link paths rely on raw curl with ATLASSIAN_EMAIL/ATLASSIAN_API_TOKEN env vars (because MCP tools do not support multipart/arbitrary POST) — so it needs those creds set to use the full flow, though it degrades gracefully if they are missing. Evals exist but there is no evidence in the diff that they have been run/passed.
prResults.relevanceToRefinement: Conference features come from JIRA backlog tickets and the loop ends in an explicit Share stage, so a handover/resume pair maps directly onto persisting work back to the ticket and picking it up later. Strong fit for the Share step and for cross-session continuity during a time-boxed event (push, draft PR, attach context, comment — then resume). It is a session-continuity / wrap-up tool rather than something that drives the core Research / Plan / Build work itself, so it is highly useful at the bookends but not central to the build loop. Caveat: requires Atlassian API creds for the full attachment flow.

prResults.title: feat(mine-pr-case-studies): add multi-lens PR case study skill
prResults.whatItAdds: Adds a new skill `mine-pr-case-studies` to the `experimental-skills` plugin (bumps it 0.2.0 -> 0.3.0). It is a retrospective analysis tool: it mines historical merged PRs for a *repeated* engineering operation and builds evidence-based case studies + a synthesis report from git/GitHub signals (correction commits, reviewer-triggered fixes, CI failures, time-to-merge, AI-assisted flag, cohort year), never from recollection/inference. It supports five selectable lenses via a `LENS` parameter sharing one discovery+extraction pipeline: friction (default; pain points + guide-gap analysis), best-practices (exemplar PRs), evolution (per-year cohort trends), ai-vs-human (AI vs human PR comparison), compliance (rule-adherence scorecard via grep RULE_PATTERNS over diffs). It runs a 3-phase loop (Discovery -> per-PR case study -> Synthesis), validates required params per lens before any command runs, and explicitly stops at writing synthesis.md (does not edit guides or open PRs). Notably, every validated config and all evals are go-sdk-ios module-creation specific (KEYWORD='Init TomTomSDK', podspec/xcworkspace/domain_to_module_mapping.yml), so it is tuned to a particular repeated SDK operation rather than generic feature work.
prResults.readyToUse: Well-developed and well-tested but NOT ready to grab: PR is still OPEN (unmerged), and it lands in a plugin explicitly named/described as personal + experimental ("Personal plugin for experimental and cross-cutting Claude Code skills", author Borys Zhdanov). The skill itself is mature — 511-line SKILL.md, README, 13 evals covering all 5 lenses, missing-parameter guards, plus a deterministic end-to-end mock-execution harness (stub gh/git scripts + canned PR JSON). So: experimental/early in availability, but the content quality is high.
prResults.relevanceToRefinement: Low relevance to the conference Pick -> Research -> Plan -> Build -> Verify -> Share loop. This is a retrospective process-analysis tool, not a feature-building aid. Hard disqualifier for the Build use case: the skill requires a corpus of 5+ historical PRs of the *same repeated operation* and is explicitly "not applicable" below that — a team refining/building one fresh backlog feature has no such corpus. The only thread is a squint-fit to the Research phase (understanding how an existing process performs / where friction lives), and even that is about improving a process, not researching a specific feature. It does not help Plan, Build, Verify, or Share a single feature. iOS-SDK-specific tuning further narrows applicability.

prResults.title: refactor(splitting-big-prs): extract phases to references/ for progressive disclosure
prResults.whatItAdds:
This PR does NOT add a new skill/capability — it refactors the EXISTING `splitting-big-prs` skill (in the `pr-tooling` plugin). The skill already exists and works; it converts one large PR/branch into a chain of small, stacked, individually-buildable PRs, enforcing an "Iron Law" that the final increment's diff is byte-identical to the original big branch.

The actual delta in this PR (per the diff, SKILL.md: +17/-294):
1. Progressive-disclosure restructuring — the four phase procedures (Phase 0 Pre-flight, 1 Plan, 2 Per-Increment Loop, 3 Final Validation) are moved verbatim out of SKILL.md into four new reference files under `references/phases/phase-{0-3}-*.md`. SKILL.md drops from ~5,451 to ~2,150 words; it keeps a Phases table pointing to each file via `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}`, and keeps the pressure-bearing content inline (Iron Law, Core Invariants, flow diagram, sizing heuristics, rationalizations table, red flags).
2. A hard forcing function added to the Phases section: "Before executing a phase, read its reference file in full. If you have not read the phase reference file, STOP — do not improvise from this overview."
3. Five minor content fixes folded in: a new "What This Doesn't Cover" section (uncommitted work, already-merged commits, non-stacked parallel PRs, multi-repo, rewriting the big branch); a worked E2E-test-placement example in Phase 1; a rebase-cost tradeoff clause for the top-down DI+fakes strategy; `BASE_OF_INCREMENT` turned into a copy-paste-runnable assignment in Phase 2; and clarifying comments on the Phase 3 backfill loop.

Behavior is preserved: phase numbering and cross-references are unchanged, and the 11 behavioral evals in evals/evals.json are untouched.
prResults.readyToUse: Mature/production, and this PR is a non-functional refactor. The skill is not a draft (isDraft: false, state OPEN) and is usable today. This PR is behavior-preserving polish — content moved verbatim into reference files, evals unchanged at 11, cross-references grep-verified per the PR body. So "ready to use" applies to the skill itself; the PR is a maintenance/quality change, not a new feature.
prResults.relevanceToRefinement: Low-to-niche for the conference's Pick -> Research -> Plan -> Build -> Verify -> Share loop. This is a Share-stage tool with a deliberately narrow trigger ("Use when the user explicitly asks to split/break up/decompose a big PR"). Whether it helps depends on whether a time-boxed conference team produces a branch large enough to need stacked decomposition — usually they won't in a single event. And this specific PR's delta (a progressive-disclosure refactor) adds nothing an attendee using the skill would notice; the underlying skill, not this PR, is what would matter. Useful as a reference example of a well-structured discipline-enforcing skill (good model for teams writing their own skills), but not a capability most refinement teams will reach for during the event.

prResults.title: feat: add direnv-tools plugin with external-env skill
prResults.whatItAdds: Adds a new `direnv-tools` plugin to the marketplace containing one skill, `external-env`. The skill centralizes a repo's environment variables in a file outside the project tree at `~/.config/direnv/<org>/<project>/.env`, keyed by the Git `origin` remote slug, so secrets/local-only vars never live inside the repo. A deterministic `setup.sh` (covering steps C1-C4): checks direnv is installed, idempotently installs a global `direnvrc` hook (`_load_external_repo_env`) that auto-loads the `.env` on `cd` into any clone of the repo (no project `.envrc` needed), derives+validates the slug from the remote URL, and creates the `.env` if missing. The SKILL.md then detects project type and offers four integration paths so the same central `.env` is consumed by: (A) a project direnv `.envrc`, (B) Gradle/spring-dotenv via `springdotenv.directory`, (C) Python/python-dotenv via `load_dotenv(...)`, and (D) CMake via either a `null`-valued `CMakePresets.json` environment block or a `LoadCentralEnv.cmake` module that reads KEY=VALUE pairs at configure time. Security-conscious throughout: never reads/prints existing `.env` contents, validates the slug against path traversal, and never embeds secret values in committed project files.
prResults.readyToUse: Early/experimental but functionally complete. Plugin version is 0.1.0, the PR is OPEN and NOT a draft, and the entire test plan is unchecked (no boxes ticked) — so nothing has been verified yet, including `/plugin validate .`, install, slug derivation, and hook idempotency. The shell script uses `set -euo pipefail`, an idempotent hook install, slug regex validation and traversal guard, so the core is reasonably robust, but it is unmerged and untested. Caveats noted in the diff: requires direnv 2.21+ for absolute-path `dotenv`; the hook's sed pattern and the C3 slug derivation are duplicated and must be kept in sync manually; double-loading is possible (but harmless) if both the global hook and an `.envrc` are used.
prResults.relevanceToRefinement: Moderately relevant as supporting tooling rather than a core part of the Pick->Research->Plan->Build->Verify->Share loop. At the Build/Verify stage, a real backlog feature often needs API keys, DB URLs, or service tokens to run and test locally; this skill gives a clean, secret-safe, one-command way to wire those into the shell, Gradle, Python, or CMake builds without committing them or hand-rolling an `.envrc`. That removes a common friction point when actually running the feature during the conference. It does not help with the AI-driven refinement/research/planning itself, and it only matters once a team reaches the run-it-locally step — and only for repos that need env vars. So it is a genuine convenience for hands-on building but tangential to the refinement workflow the track is centered on.
